characteristics.harvestSeason: First flush, after 2–3 weeks of shading

description.short: Japan's most prestigious whole-leaf green tea — heavily shaded before harvest, brimming with deep savory umami sweetness
description.overview: Like matcha, gyokuro employs extensive canopy shading before picking, but retains the intact whole needle leaf rather than stone-grinding, creating a concentrated, broth-like elixir.
description.liquor: Pale jade-gold to rich crystalline green
description.aroma: Heady oceanic umami, roasted nori, sweet steamed greens
description.taste: Explosive broth-like umami, velvety sweetness, minimal bitterness when brewed with low water temperatures
description.aftertaste: Deeply savory, coating, enduring umami finish
description.processing: Intense canopy shading for 2–3 weeks → hand or careful machine plucking → steam fixation → intricate needle rolling → drying

history.origin: Gyokuro was created in Uji in the 1830s as a development of the shading technique previously reserved for ceremonial tencha, adapting it to whole-leaf infusion.
history.development: Yame on the southern island of Kyushu became a world capital of gyokuro alongside Uji, celebrated for its river mists and specialized straw shading screens (honzu).
history.modern: Gyokuro represents the absolute pinnacle of Japanese loose-leaf tea in price, rarity, and craftsmanship, celebrated like fine vintage wine.
interestingFacts: The name translates as 'Jade Dew', referring to the pale, luminescent jade droplets in the cup.
Brewed at just 50–60°C (122–140°F), gyokuro has one of the lowest brewing temperatures of any tea in the world, specifically designed to extract theanine without releasing bitter catechins.
